questions.text: Consider a CSMA/CD network that transmits data at a rate of 100 Mbps ([latex]10^{8}[/latex] bits per second) over a 1 km (kilometer) cable with no repeaters. If the minimum frame size required for this network is 1250 bytes, what is the signal speed (km/sec) in the cable?
questions.solution:
CSMA/CD needs [latex]T_t\ge2T_p[/latex]:
[latex]\frac{1250\times8}{10^8}=100\,\mu s=2T_p\Rightarrow T_p=50\,\mu s[/latex]

Speed = 1 km / 50 [latex]\mu s[/latex] = 20000 km/s

Answer: 20000

questions.text:
Consider the following statements.
I. TCP connections are full duplex
II. TCP has no option for selective acknowledgement
III. TCP connections are message streams
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- I: TCP connections are full duplex [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] True
- II: TCP has a SACK (selective acknowledgement) option [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] False
- III: TCP is a byte stream, not a message stream [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] False

Answer: Only I is correct

options: Only I and III are correct
Only II and III are correct
All of I, II and III are correct

questions.text: Assume that the bandwidth for a TCP connection is 1048560 bits/sec. Let [latex]\alpha[/latex] be the value of RTT in milliseconds (rounded off to the nearest integer) after which the TCP window scale option is needed. Let [latex]\beta[/latex] be the maximum possible window size with window scale option. Then the values of [latex]\alpha[/latex] and [latex]\beta[/latex] are
questions.solution:
Without scaling, max window = 65535 bytes. Bandwidth = 1048560 / 8 = 131070 bytes/s.

Scaling is needed once bandwidth [latex]\times[/latex] RTT exceeds 65535: RTT = 65535 / 131070 = 0.5 s = 500 ms.

The max scale shift is 14, so [latex]\beta=65535\times2^{14}[/latex].

Answer: 500 milliseconds, 65535 [latex]\times[/latex] [latex]2^{14}[/latex]

questions.text: Host A sends a UDP datagram containing 8880 bytes of user data to host B over an Ethernet LAN. Ethernet frames may carry data up to 1500 bytes (i.e. MTU=1500 bytes). Size of UDP header is 8 bytes and size of IP header is 20 bytes. There is no option field in IP header. How many total number of IP fragments will be transmitted and what will be the contents of offset field in the last fragment?
questions.solution:
IP payload = 8880 + 8 (UDP header) = 8888 bytes. Max data per fragment = 1500 [latex]-[/latex] 20 = 1480.

6 fragments carry 6 [latex]\times[/latex] 1480 = 8880 bytes, and 8 bytes remain [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 7 fragments.

Offset of the last = 8880 / 8 = 1110

Answer: 7 and 1110

questions.text:
Consider the following routing table at an IP router:

For each IP address in Group I identify the correct choice of the next hop from Group II using the entries from the routing table above.
questions.solution:
AND the address with each mask and look for the longest match:

- i) 171 AND 254 = 170 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Interface 0 (a)
- ii) 167 AND 254 = 166 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] R2 (c)
- iii) 163: /23 gives 162, /22 gives 160, no match [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] default R4 (e)
- iv) 165: /23 gives 164 (no /23 entry), /22 gives 164 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] R3 (d)

Answer: i-a, ii-c, iii-e, iv-d
